Question: The movie Furiosa just flopped despite rave reviews from Rotten Tomatoes and film critics. Why are film critics/enthusiasts often so out of touch with what general audiences want to see in a film?
Answer: Misplaced apathy Furiosa is the collateral victim of an ill advised, deliberate audience alienating marketing campaign Hollywood has been conducting for more than a decade now. There are plenty of reasons coming together to create the recent string of flopping projects initially expected to be hits (Furiosa, The Fall Guy, Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes), but the one I want to elaborate on is the cloud of apathy covering the general moviegoers crowd. To explain this point, I first have to give a short summary of Hollywood’s more recent marketing schemes and how they terribly and predictably backfired. For the better part of the last decade, in a majority of cases concerning popular action, adventure and fantasy franchises, studio executives decided it’s not right for their predominant viewership to be male. To correct this travesty, they proudly initiated a string of projects and aggressive marketing campaigns meant to skew the viewer demographic more towards a female audience. We got the president of Marvel Studios saying the MCU will have more female than male superheroes[1], the president of Lucas Films complaining that Star Wars is underperforming due to the fanbase being too male dominated[2]and calling for more female representation[3], we have newer shows like The Witcher altering the source material to shift more focus on female characters[4]and the list goes on. Now, there is nothing wrong with expanding to new demographics and increasing female lead roles per se. That’s a decision that makes perfect sense. However, it quickly becomes clear the goal was not to expand to new demographics, it was to replace the existing one. Two actions were taken in parallel, one more successful than the other. Alienating the male audience On one side, studios started moving away from male moviegoers by injecting preachiness and male hating rhetoric in a bunch of projects, with a special target on franchises popular with the demographic. Writers started peppering movies with lines about how masculinity is toxic and how men are oppressive, inferior creatures that need to “do better”. We have the new female Dr. Who referring to her gender as “an upgrade”, we have Batgirl saying the batsuit will only be perfect “when it fits a woman”, we have She Hulk with the superpower of complaining about men every other line of her entire show, and many more. We even got a ton of legacy shattering prequels, sequels and reboots that either make the original male characters look like complete idiots or replace them with female counterparts. Han Solo is now a deadbeat dad who needs Ray to show him how operate his own ship, Indiana Jones is a sad old man who gets outsmarted by Helena at every step, and pretty much every male Marvel superhero is playing second fiddle to their female counterparts while being reduced to walking punchlines. On top of this, producers and actors adjacent to these projects got directives to make their reluctance towards male viewers clear with every chance they got. It became very common in interviews to state how proud everyone is to be moving away from them. Everything “non-male” was marketed as a sign of evolution. Mind you this is for the more classy cases. The less classy, well…we have the self proclaimed activist director of upcoming Star Wars Rey movie saying “I love to make men uncomfortable” or Captain Marvel’s Brie Larson saying “I don’t need a 40 year old white dude telling me what they think, it’s not for them”. All in all, the vibe has been unnecessarily mean towards male fans. Of course, not all studios are partaking in this (more on that later), but the guilty parties are responsible for some of the most popular franchises ever and cover a major part of Hollywood output. The tone they set quickly contaminates everything in the space. After years of hammering it home, the message was finally received. Male audiences became apathetic or downright defensive. Their assumption became that any new project from popular action adventure franchises is deliberately made to be unappealing to them. This part of the plan worked. Part two however was not so successful. Attracting a larger female audience Once the men have safely been removed from the premises, studios went on to filling the now open seats with female viewers. The plan for that was simple. Good old fashion pandering. They started creating more and more female characters, gender swapping old male ones and started spreading the word that these franchises - which were never gendered, by the way - now belong to women. The acting, writing, directing and production staffs have been made more and more “female centered”. That is not a negative on it’s own. The issue however is that this was the main and often times only focus point of the marketing campaigns: we have women in our show, so women will flock to see them regardless of quality, was the logic. I’m not sure if this level of pandering is more or less insulting then what they did to their male audience, but that is a topic for another answer. The point is, it didn’t work. Take The Marvels for example. All female cast, all female writing staff and female director. On paper, it was the completion of this grand masterplan. The moment when superhero movie audiences become predominantly female. The Marvels lost $237 million[5]. And here’s the kicker. 68% of the audience was still male[6]. The same thing happened over and over again, with most Disney’s Star Wars movies[7], Madame Web[8], Doctor Who[9], The Witcher[10], The Rings of Power[11], and pretty much any project that adhered to this disastrous strategy. The funny part is, even after the data was in, many refuse to see what was right in front of them. This tweet from one of Jimmy Fallon’s writers pretty much sums up the attitude of many in Hollywood: Of course it’s the consumers fault Many turned to their favorite hobby - crapping on potential male fans. In a fascinating feat of mental gymnastics, men are to blame for the failure of these movies even though they still make up more than 50% of the audience[12]. The failure of shows geared to appeal to women are failing because men are not supporting them more. At no point during this backpedaling has the lack of female viewers ever been brought up, which takes me to my next point. Demographics The demographics of different movie genres has to do with inherent preferences, and is not something that can be socially engineered in an impactful way. Women will not flock to see a movie from a genre they are not interested in to begin with just because the lead and director are female. Action adventure movies skew towards male audiences, just how romantic comedies and musicals skew towards female ones. There is as much chance of creating a predominantly female audience for action movies as you have of creating a predominantly straight male audience for Barbie or Fifty Shades of Grey. It’s a fools errand, and Hollywood’s activitst experiment proves it. The male audience has been put off, while the female audience is made up of the same women that were happy going to see Iron Man and The Phantom Menace. To sum up, in what will probably go down as the most counterproductive movement in the history of any entertainment industry, Hollywood successfully alienated well over 50% of their audience and did nothing of note to expand on the remaining one. Now, you might say “if these movies were actually well written, people would have gone to see them”. Fully agreed! But the majority of the audience would still be male, as will always be the case with action adventure franchises. And speaking of well written movies: This finally brings me to Furiosa. This is a well written, well acted movie with a compelling story and world build that would delight almost anyone who is interested in the genre, and beyond. There is no obvious reason why it should flop. It’s actually one of the few recent examples where both critics and audiences agree. The reason it flopped is not because it’s not a good movie. It’s because audiences did not even give it a chance. The average moviegoer saw the trailer, saw what looked like another popular franchise getting rebooted with a gender-swapped lead, and decided it’s likely another legacy shattering, pandering piece of activist material that is not made for their genuine entertainment. Add the increased ticket price and the convenience of streaming services and it’s easy to see why many people thought it’s not worth the risk. I will reiterate, Furiosa is a good movie. The movie itself and the marketing leading up to it are not guilty of any of the sins I listed above. It’s just an innocent victim, caught in the blast radius of an activist marketing stunt carried out by others in the same space. And it’s a damn shame.

Question: What do you consider cringe?
Answer: Influencers in public spaces The best place to witness this cringe inducing lack of self awareness is Oia. A beautiful village in Santorini, ruined by it’s status as one of the worlds most “instagramable” places. She’s asking like 50 strangers to stop just so she can take that picture Any self restraint goes out the window here. Scores of instagram “models” cover every vantage point, like pigeons flocking to crap on a statue. They take dozens of pictures in cringey, seductive poses, while large queues of people are waiting for their turn at pretending to live in luxury for internet fame. Each one accompanied by a bored looking boyfriend with matching clothes, who’s now wondering if the sex is worth it. People waiting in line for pictures On our visit, we saw two ladies get into a screaming match because one was hogging the spot for too long. Another one had a professional photographer. She claimed an entire intersection to herself, barking at anyone who was passing through as if it was a movie set. Another lady had a gym-bag full of dresses. She would take a picture, then change outfits in the middle of the street. All under the frustrated eyes of a couple dozen people eager to take her spot. It’s hard work, feeding ones ego.

Name: Michael Strauss
Question: What movie scene was the hardest/most uncomfortable to watch?
Answer: Squeal like a pig - Deliverance (1972) I won’t go into details describing this scene as I’m not up for publicly unpacking childhood traumas on Quora. In terms of brutally disturbing sexual assaults, what sets this one apart is the sheer added humiliation of Ned Beatty’s character. On top of being assaulted in front of his friends, he is made to crawl on all four, imitating barn animals that his assailant likely has sex with on a regular basis. As effective and memorable - in a scarring way - as this scene is, I never understood what could possess an actor to sign up for it, even if it meant playing alongside the likes of Jon Voight and Burt Reynolds. It’s one of those scenes that will follow one to the grave. Roger from American Dad said it best: “Poor Ned Beatty. He can play Rudy’s dad all he wants, all we see when we look at him is him getting rammed in the woods”

Name: Michael Strauss
Question: What's the saddest episode of a comedy TV show?
Answer: And Maggie Makes Three - The Simpsons The episode is Homer telling Lisa and Bart the story of why there are no baby pictures of Maggie in the family photo album. The story starts with Homer quitting his job at the power plant to finally pursue his dream: working at the bowling alley. Ending the job that made him miserable so many years goes exactly how you’d expect. Homer accepts a lower paycheck, but for the first time in his professional life he is actually happy. In the meantime, Marge gets pregnant with Maggie. A surprise for the couple, this pregnancy comes with serious financial strain. They can not afford to raise three children on his new salary. After trying every possible, shenanigans filled angle to increase his income, Homer finally realizes he has only one choice. Give up his dreams and return to the place that made him miserable. Homer is made to beg for his old job back, Mr. Burns taking complete advantage to humiliate and further break him. In a twisted display of sadism, he installs a plaque above Homer’s desk, to remind him of his place. Homer will never dare hope at happiness again. “So, why no pictures?” - Bart asks, as Homer is telling his story. “Oh, there are pictures. I keep them where I need the most cheering up” I’m not crying, you’re crying!

Question: To win 3 billion dollars, you have to survive 24 hours getting chased by a horror villain of your choice. Who are you picking?
Answer: Esther from Orphan If you don’t know this movie (spoilers incoming), Orphan is about a family who - devastated after the loss of their child - decide to adopt Esther, a nine year old girl from an orphanage. Name: Michael Strauss
Question: What movie could have been over in 10 minutes if the main character wasn't such a fool?
Answer: The Cabin in the Woods Not the main character, but “The Director”, who is the mastermind of the entire operation. The Cabin in the Woods is meant more as a tongue in cheek commentary of horror movies that pokes fun at all the recognizable tropes, used to death in the last few decades. It’s meant to be a comedy/satire that takes us through Hollywood’s age old recipe for slasher films, but I will treat it as a very serious plan of action for when humanity is in that actual situation. I’ve come up with the perfect solution, but first a quick summary. The movie follows a stereotypical group of five college students on a weekend trip to an also stereotypical cabin. They discover a basement full of stereotypical, creepy, obviously cursed items, which of course they touch, thus summoning some random movie monsters bent on killing them all. In their attempts to get away, the two remaining students discover an entire facility hiding under the cabin, housing all sorts of familiar horror creatures. The facility is ran like a run of the mill corporation, complete with bored employees who do raffles and presumably have casual Fridays and play bullshit bingo during company update calls. The purpose of this organization is to annually sacrifice five archetypes to some mean gods that will otherwise destroy all of humanity. The CEO of this whole endeavor - which I would argue is the single most important job in the world - is The Director. Her plan all along has been to lure potential sacrifices and to orchestrate the order in which they die. And here’s the problem. She was trying to trick people into being sacrifice. People are not very keen on that. Instead, it could have been done on a volunteer basis. Hear me out. Make it a game-show! Five categories, one for each archetype: Whores (God knows there’s plenty reality TV already in this segment), Athletes, Scholars, Fools and Virgins. Send them in the cabin, unleash the monsters and whoever can survive the weekend gets a million dollars and becomes instantly famous. The whole thing is financed via live streaming and sponsorships, like the Olympics. To make it more interesting, randomly drop weapons like in a game of Fortnite. Or make them answer trivia questions for “1 hour in the safe room”. Be creative. Let the Japanese make the rules Who wouldn’t tune in to see that? And before you think people would not sign up for this, come on…we’ve all seen Squid Game. What wouldn’t people do for fame and fortune?
